title: How do we sort the fractions into two groups by length?
description: The fractions marked earlier on the number lines are sorted into lengths less than one unit and lengths more than one unit. The board checks where each line ends against the mark one and counts that no fraction is left out. Keeko doubts that seven eighths is more than one.
teaching_notes: One idea: a line is less than one unit if it ends before the mark one, and more than one unit if it ends after it. Watch for students who judge a fraction by how big its numbers look.

source: Write down all the fractions you marked on the number line earlier
video_script.why: A learner sorts fractions into those shorter and those longer than one unit by looking at where each line ends.
video_script.substitution: the book's own fractions marked earlier on the number lines
video_script.anchor: the number lines from the last section with their blue lines and black lines
video_script.wrong_answer: seven eighths is more than one, because seven and eight are big numbers
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko judges a fraction by how big its numbers look and not by where its line ends.
video_script.payoff_line: The blue lengths are less than one unit, and the black lengths are more than one unit

final_answer.spoken: the blue lengths are less than one unit, and the black lengths are more than one unit

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, one third, two thirds, one fifth, seven eighths, one tenth, three tenths, three halves, six fifths, seven fifths, eight fifths, nine fifths
maths_rules: a line from 0 is less than 1 unit if it ends before the mark 1
a line from 0 is more than 1 unit if it ends after the mark 1
video_script.design: The earlier number lines shown together. Each line is compared with the mark one and moved into one of two boxes.

<bookmark mark='boxes'/>We must sort the fractions into two groups.
How can we tell which fraction goes in which group?

narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>The mark one is the end of one whole unit.
<bookmark mark='beyond'/>A line that ends after the mark one is longer than one unit.

beats.on_screen: Check: 16 + 5 = 21, so no fraction is left out

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>To check, sixteen and five make twenty one. That is every line, and none is left out.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The blue lengths are less than one unit, and the black lengths are more than one unit.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks seven eighths is more than one, because seven and eight are big numbers.
<bookmark mark='short'/>But the line of seven eighths stops one part before the mark one.
